decisions.description: Withdrawals are capped at a daily limit of 5000 per account, a value the plan never mentions.
The 'daily' withdrawal total is never reset, so the cap is effectively a lifetime limit per ledger instance.
Only withdrawals count toward the daily limit; outgoing transfers are not limited.
Amounts are rounded to two decimal places (cents) using Math.round, i.e. half-up toward positive infinity, with floating-point error.
The positive-amount check runs before rounding, so a tiny positive amount such as 0.004 is accepted and recorded as a zero-value operation.
Balances are stored as floating-point numbers and sums are not re-rounded, so cent errors can accumulate.
Overdrafts are forbidden: a withdrawal or transfer that would make the balance negative is rejected with 'insufficient-funds'.
When a withdrawal both exceeds the balance and the daily limit, insufficient funds is reported first.
A repeated transaction id is acknowledged as success and ignored, without checking that the account, amount or operation type match the original.
Transaction ids share one global namespace across all accounts and operation types.
Only accepted operations mark their transaction id as seen, so retrying a rejected id can later succeed as a new operation.
Amount validation happens before the duplicate check, so a retry with an invalid amount is rejected rather than acknowledged.
Infinity passes the positive-amount check and is accepted, while NaN is rejected.
Accounts are created implicitly with a zero balance on first use by any operation, including withdrawals and transfers that are then rejected.
An explicit public open() method exists and is a no-op for an existing account.
Querying the balance of an unknown account returns 0 instead of an error.
Querying the history of an unknown account returns an empty list instead of an error.
Account ids and transaction ids are not validated, so empty or arbitrary strings are accepted.
Rejections are returned as {ok:false, reason} values with fixed reason strings rather than thrown errors.
A transfer is recorded as two history entries, transfer-out and transfer-in, sharing the same transaction id and a positive amount.
